analysis.one_liner: Phases out nonessential 'forever chemicals' from products, manufacturing, and environmental releases over ten years.
analysis.headline: A bill to phase out 'forever chemicals' has sat in five House committees since its March 2026 introduction, with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS ('forever chemicals') are long-lasting industrial chemicals linked to health problems that have contaminated drinking water across the country. This bill would require manufacturers and users of PFAS to report their uses and releases annually, ban a list of PFAS-containing consumer products within one to five years, and require a full phaseout of all nonessential PFAS uses and releases within ten years, with 'essential uses' (critical uses with no safer alternative) allowed to continue. It gives the EPA inspection and penalty authority, lets citizens sue violators, makes federal agencies follow the same PFAS rules as private companies, and changes bankruptcy and state-law rules so people exposed to toxic chemicals can still pursue damages.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink contaminated water, live near PFAS release sites, or buy PFAS-containing products. The bill would reduce exposure to chemicals that persist in the body and environment, create a public record of who uses and releases PFAS, restore the ability to sue for exposure damages, and create research centers focused on PFAS remediation, including one focused on rural water sources.

how_it_helps.text: Bans the sale of PFAS-containing carpets, food packaging, cosmetics, apparel, furniture, and juvenile products within one to five years, and requires a full phaseout of all nonessential PFAS uses within ten years [S3].

Makes it unlawful after ten years for manufacturers or users to release any detectable amount of PFAS into the environment, and requires federal agencies to stop buying products known to contain PFAS [S2].
Requires annual public reporting by every PFAS manufacturer and user, covering volumes, releases, health effects, and the number of workers exposed, increasing transparency for the public [S3].
Allows citizen lawsuits against PFAS makers, users, and the EPA, and addresses state-law damages claims and bankruptcy rules so exposure victims can pursue companies for harm [S2].

Waives federal immunity so government agencies are subject to the same PFAS regulations and penalties as private parties, with only narrow, renewable national-security exemptions the President must report to Congress [S3].

analysis.who_pays: PFAS manufacturers (including importers and exporters) and companies that use PFAS in consumer products, which would face reporting fees, phaseout costs, enforcement penalties, and litigation exposure. Some costs could be passed to consumers through prices for products like apparel and outdoor gear, though the bill's essential-use process allows chemicals to remain where no safer alternative exists.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical makers and PFAS-using product companies

drawbacks.text: Transition costs for manufacturers and users of PFAS, which could raise prices for goods like clothing, cosmetics, and furniture during the phaseout [S3].

Essential-use designations cannot begin until after the National Academies completes a review (up to three years) and submits a report plus one year, so the designation process starts late relative to the ten-year phaseout deadline, creating uncertainty for companies and regulators [S3].

Some PFAS uses in medicine, electronics, and industry have no proven safer alternative; the bill handles this with an essential-use process, but a poorly run process could either block needed products or leave health risks in place [S3].
Compliance costs fall on many small firms as well as large chemical companies, though the bill allows reduced fees for small manufacturers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case is strong: PFAS persist in the environment and human bodies and are widespread in drinking water, so reducing releases and nonessential uses addresses a real, long-lasting harm. The bill is gradual, with ten-year timelines, essential-use exemptions, and resale exceptions for used goods, which limits disruption. The main weaknesses are the slow start of the essential-use designation process and compliance burdens spread across many businesses, but the bill's structure gives regulators and companies a decade to find alternatives. The costs fall mainly on the chemical and consumer-products industries rather than on households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to five House committees, and after one subcommittee referral it has not moved; it is waiting to see if any committee acts on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Betty McCollum (D-MN), joined by Rep. Kelly Morrison, introduced the Forever Chemical Regulation and Accountability Act of 2026 in the House on March 19, 2026 [S1].
The bill was referred to five committees: Energy and Commerce, Oversight and Government Reform, Science, Space and Technology, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Armed Services [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, and no further action appears in the record [S5].
Seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].

The bill would phase out nonessential PFAS uses over ten years, ban PFAS in listed consumer products within one to five years, give the EPA enforcement authority, allow citizen suits, and make federal agencies comply with PFAS rules [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, PFAS manufacturers and the consumer-product companies that use the chemicals, which continue operating under existing rules while the bill sits without committee action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical makers and PFAS-using companies, for now

for.name: Rep. Betty McCollum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase out nonessential PFAS uses and releases [S3].

for.name: Rep. Kelly Morrison
for.role: Original cosponsor, U.S. House of Representatives (MN)

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Controls committee schedules and the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: No committee chaired by the majority has scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since its referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat (8 of 217 House Democrats), with no Republican support on the record so far.

industries.note: The bill requires annual reporting with fees (a $100,000 default fee if the EPA misses its deadline), a ten-year phaseout of nonessential production, a ban on detectable releases, and citizen-suit and criminal enforcement exposure. Their continued sales of PFAS impose contamination and health costs on the public [S3].

industries.industry: Consumer product makers (apparel, cosmetics, food packaging, carpets, furniture, juvenile products)
industries.note: The bill bans sale of PFAS-containing versions of these products within one to five years, forcing reformulation; used-item resale is exempted. Their interest in continuing to use PFAS runs against the public's interest in reducing exposure [S3].
The bill establishes Centers of Excellence for PFAS water assessment and remediation and declares destruction and remediation a national priority, creating research and cleanup demand [S3].

industries.industry: Public water utilities and waste treatment operators
industries.note: They are expressly excluded from the definitions of manufacturer and user, so they avoid direct liability and reporting duties, while source-pollution controls and remediation reduce the contamination they must treat [S3].

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and a House majority controlled by the other party, the bill faces long odds: it sits in five committees, any one of which could stop it, and the great majority of bills never receive a hearing or vote. Unless a committee acts soon, it will likely die at the end of this Congress in January 2027.
